How I Did It: Galaxy Raiders

by Sal, Galaxy Zone Arcade

Sal remembers the original cabinet

Galaga came in during the good years, '82 or so, and it split the whole arcade into two kinds of people: the ones who just wanted to shoot bugs, and the ones who'd stand there for twenty minutes practicing how to lose a ship to the tractor beam on purpose. There was a kid — I want to say his name was Denny — who fed that machine every quarter he made mowing lawns all summer just to get good enough at winning his ship back. Never once asked me for a refund when the coin slot jammed, which it did constantly. He'd just bang the side of the cabinet twice, like it owed him an apology, and it usually paid up.

What the remodel changed

Last year I had those bug formations just marching in a straight line because that's all I knew how to make them do. This time the robots showed me something called a "bezier curve" — which sounds fancier than it is, it's just a fancy way of drawing a swoop instead of a straight line, and it's timed off the actual clock instead of counting frames, so it swoops the same whether your computer's fast or slow. That's how the whole squadron flies in from the corners now, curving into formation instead of just popping into place. And the tractor beam — that's the one I really wanted right — the boss dives down, throws that cone of light, and if it catches you, you lose your ship and watch it ride back up docked on that same bug, mad as anything. Shoot that bug later while it's out on another dive and you get your pilot back, and suddenly you've got two ships flying side by side firing together. I made them shake the screen and flash the whole thing cyan when that happens. Wasn't in the plan. It should've been from the start.

The spell that did it

Build Galaxy Raiders against our GZ engine. Formation of bees, butterflies, and boss galaga that fly in on curved paths and settle into a swaying grid, then peel off in small groups to dive and shoot at the player. Give the boss galaga a real tractor beam: it dives to mid-screen, casts a cone, and captures the player ship if it connects — losing a life and docking the ship on that boss. Shooting that specific boss on a later dive should free the captured ship and turn the player into a dual fighter with double shots. Every third stage should be a no-shooting bonus wave with a perfect-clear bonus. Make the capture and rescue feel huge — flash, shake, particles, the works.

Under the hood

  • The whole stage runs off one accumulated clock, not a frame count, so every swoop — entrance, dive, tractor beam, the loop back to formation — is a curve sampled against real seconds, not guesswork.
  • The tractor beam is its own little state machine on the boss: dive down, hover and cast the cone, then loop back up, whether or not it actually caught you.
  • A boss remembers if it's holding your ship. Land a hit on that exact boss while it's out diving — before the beam or after — and it lets your pilot go and you're flying double.
  • Every third stage swaps out the shooting for a flythrough — no return fire, just score what you can before they're gone, and a fat bonus if you don't let a single one get past you.
